We both loved Adrian, though she was still a child and could not appreciate his many good qualities as I did, or share my understanding of his interests and opinions. I was always with him. His sensitive, gentle nature gave our conversations a tenderness that seemed beyond this world. At other times he was as cheerful as a lark singing high in the sky, his thoughts soaring like an eagle, his innocence that of a soft-eyed dove. He could lighten Perdita’s solemn mood and soothe the restless energy that tormented me. I looked back on my frustrated desires and painful struggles with other people as though they were a troubled dream. I felt as changed as if I had entered a different body, whose new senses and nerves made the entire world appear differently in my mind. Yet that was not so. My strength was unchanged, as were my deep need for understanding and my longing to act. My manly qualities had not left me: the enchantress Urania had spared Samson’s hair while he rested at her feet. But everything in me had grown gentler and more humane. Nor did Adrian teach me only the dry facts of history and philosophy. As he used them to help me master my own reckless, untaught spirit, he also opened the living book of his heart to me, allowing me to feel and understand its remarkable nature.

Even when her son was an infant, the former queen of England had tried to fill his mind with bold and ambitious plans. She recognised his genius and exceptional gifts, and developed them so that she could later use them to advance her own purposes. She encouraged his hunger for knowledge and his headlong courage. She even accepted his fierce love of freedom, hoping that, as so often happens, it would grow into a desire to command others. She tried to raise him to resent those who had helped bring about his father’s abdication and to want revenge on them. Here she failed. However distorted the accounts he received, the story of a great and wise nation demanding the right to govern itself inspired his admiration. From an early age he believed in a republic on principle. Still, his mother refused to give up hope. Alongside her love of power and proud sense of royal birth, she possessed firm ambition, patience, and self-control. She devoted herself to understanding her son’s character. Through praise, criticism, and urging, she tried to find the right strings to touch. Although the music her touch produced sounded wrong to her, she placed her hopes in his talents, confident that she would eventually win him over.

‘This must have been at just that stage of Mr Elliot’s life,’ said Anne, ‘which has always particularly aroused my curiosity. It must have been near the time when my father and sister first knew him. I had no acquaintance with him myself; I heard only reports; but something in his behaviour towards my father and sister then, and later in the circumstances attending his marriage, has always seemed to me difficult to reconcile with the present. It suggested quite another kind of man.’

‘I know the whole of it, the whole of it,’ exclaimed Mrs Smith. ‘He had already been presented to Sir Walter and your sister when I first knew him, but he was perpetually speaking of them. I know that invitations and encouragement were offered him, and I know he preferred not to accept. Perhaps I can enlighten you upon matters you would scarcely suppose; and concerning his marriage, I knew everything at the time. I was acquainted with every argument for and against; it was to me, as his friend, that he entrusted his hopes and schemes. Though I had not known his wife beforehand—indeed, her lower station in society made that impossible—I knew her throughout her subsequent life, or at any rate until its last two years, and can reply to whatever questions you choose to ask.’

‘No,’ said Anne, ‘there is nothing particular I wish to enquire about her. I have always been told that their marriage was unhappy. But I would like to understand why, at that period, he treated my father’s acquaintance with such indifference. My father was certainly inclined to show him every kind and proper attention. Why should Mr Elliot have withdrawn?’

‘Mr Elliot,’ Mrs Smith replied, ‘had at that time a single purpose: to acquire a fortune, and somewhat faster than the law would allow him to do. He had resolved to gain it through marriage. At least, he had resolved not to spoil his prospects by marrying imprudently. And I know he believed—whether correctly or otherwise, I certainly cannot judge—that your father and sister intended, by their attentions and invitations, to arrange a marriage between the heir and the young lady. Such a union could never have met his notions of riches and independence. That, I assure you, was why he held back. He related the entire business to me. With me he kept nothing secret. It was an odd circumstance that, having only just left you in Bath, I should find your cousin my first and chief acquaintance after marrying, and through him hear continually of your father and sister.’

He made it clear that Frank admired her enormously—found her very beautiful and very charming. With so much in his favour altogether, she decided she ought not to judge him severely. As Mrs. Weston remarked, ‘All young people have their little whims.’

One of his new acquaintances in Surrey was less forgiving. Generally, throughout the parishes of Donwell and Highbury, people assessed him generously. They readily excused the small excesses of so handsome a young man, who smiled so frequently and bowed so gracefully. But one person’s critical judgment could not be softened by either bows or smiles: Mr. Knightley. He heard about the incident at Hartfield and at first said nothing. Almost immediately afterwards, however, Emma heard him mutter to himself over the newspaper in his hand, ‘Hum! Just the frivolous, foolish fellow I thought him.’ She was half inclined to take offence, but a moment’s observation persuaded her that he had spoken merely to express his own feelings, with no intention of provoking anyone, so she let it pass.

Although Mr. and Mrs. Weston had brought unwelcome news on one subject, their visit that morning proved particularly timely in another way. While they were at Hartfield, something happened that made Emma want their advice; still more fortunately, the advice they gave was precisely what she wanted.

This was what happened. The Coles had lived in Highbury for several years and were thoroughly decent people: friendly, generous, and without pretension. On the other hand, they came from humble origins, worked in trade, and had only a moderate degree of social polish. When they first moved to the country, they lived within their income, quietly entertaining few people and spending little on those occasions. But over the past year or two their means had increased considerably. The business in town had brought in larger profits, and they had prospered in general. As their wealth grew, so did their ambitions: they wanted a bigger house and more company. They expanded their home, employed more servants, and increased their spending in every direction. By now, in both wealth and style of living, they ranked behind only the family at Hartfield. Their enjoyment of company and their new dining room had led everyone to expect dinner parties, and they had already held a few, mostly for unmarried men. Emma could hardly imagine them presuming to invite the established families of highest standing—Donwell, Hartfield, or Randalls. If they did, nothing would persuade her to attend. She regretted that her father’s well-known habits would make her refusal seem less pointed than she wished.
